subjective.question: What is television production? Briefly describe its three main stages.
subjective.answer: Television production is the process of planning, recording and finishing a programme for telecast. It has three main stages: (1) Pre-production — all the preparation before recording, such as developing the idea, research, scripting, casting, budgeting, scheduling, set design and rehearsals. (2) Production — the actual shooting/recording of the programme with cameras, lights and sound, in a studio or on location. (3) Post-production — editing the recorded material, adding music, graphics, titles and voice-over, and preparing the final programme for transmission.

subjective.question: Who is a producer? Describe the main responsibilities of a television producer.
subjective.answer: The producer has the overall creative, organizational and financial control of a production. The producer develops or selects the programme idea, arranges the budget and funds, hires the key production staff and performers, supervises scripting and scheduling, coordinates with the director during recording, and remains responsible for the programme until it is completed and delivered for telecast. Producers work closely with the directors and other production staff on a shoot so that the programme is finished on time and within budget.

subjective.question: What is the role of a director in a television production?
subjective.answer: The director is responsible for the creative and visual treatment of the programme. The director interprets the script visually, plans the shots and camera positions, guides the performers, and during recording sits in the control room (PCR) giving instructions to the camera operators, the vision mixer and the floor manager so that the recorded programme matches the planned treatment.

subjective.question: Describe the duties of a floor manager during a studio production.
subjective.answer: The floor manager is the director's representative on the studio floor. The floor manager relays the director's instructions (received through talkback/headphones) to the performers and crew, cues the performers, manages the floor activities during recording, keeps the production on schedule, and ensures discipline and safety on the studio floor.

subjective.question: Name the main members of a television production team and state the function of each.
subjective.answer: The main members are: Producer (overall in charge), Director (creative/visual control), Floor Manager (coordinates the studio floor), Camera Operator (operates the camera; in a video production a camera operator is known as a television camera operator), Lighting Director (designs and controls lighting), Audio Engineer (controls sound recording and mixing), Vision Mixer Operator/Switcher (selects the camera output through the vision mixer), Boom Operator (handles the microphone boom), Script Writer (writes dialogues and scenes) and Editor (assembles the final programme in post-production).

subjective.question: Differentiate between ENG and EFP.
subjective.answer: ENG (Electronic News Gathering) is the use of portable electronic cameras and equipment to record news events quickly on location for news programmes; speed and mobility are its main features. EFP (Electronic Field Production) also uses portable equipment outside the studio, but for planned, higher-quality productions such as dramas, documentaries and sports features, where more time and control are available than in news gathering.

subjective.question: What is a camera shot? Name the basic types of camera shots.
subjective.answer: A camera shot is a single continuous view recorded by the camera. The basic types are: Extreme Long Shot (ELS), Long Shot (LS), Medium Long Shot (MLS), Medium Shot (MS), Medium Close-Up (MCU), Close-Up (CU), Extreme Close-Up (ECU), Two-Shot, Over-the-Shoulder Shot and Point of View (POV) Shot. These shots differ in how much of the subject and its setting appears in the frame.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a long shot, a medium shot and a close-up.
subjective.answer: In a long shot the subject appears small and the setting dominates the frame; it is used to show the location and the overall scene. In a medium shot the subject or actor and its setting occupy roughly equal areas in the frame, and the subject is usually shown from about the waist up. In a close-up the subject fills the frame — for a person, mainly the face — so that details and expressions are clearly seen.

subjective.question: What is a close-up? Why is a close-up used to emphasize the emotional state of a person?
subjective.answer: A close-up is a shot in which the subject fills most of the frame; for a person it shows the face in detail. Because facial expressions are seen clearly, a close-up of a person emphasizes their emotional state — feelings such as joy, fear, anger or sorrow — and helps the audience connect with the character's inner condition.

subjective.question: What is an establishing shot? What is its purpose?
subjective.answer: An establishing shot is a long or extreme long shot, usually placed at the beginning of a scene or programme, that shows the general location and setting of the action. Its purpose is to orient the audience — to tell viewers where the action is taking place and how the subjects are related to their surroundings — before closer shots are shown.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a two-shot and an over-the-shoulder shot.
subjective.answer: A two-shot frames two persons together in a single shot and is used to show their relationship and interaction. An over-the-shoulder shot is taken from behind one person's shoulder, showing that person's shoulder/back in the foreground and the other person facing the camera; it is commonly used in conversations to show both the speaker's viewpoint and the listener's reactions.

subjective.question: What is meant by 'crossing the line' in camera movements? Why should it be avoided?
subjective.answer: In camera work there is an imaginary line, called the axis of action or the 180-degree line, drawn through the subjects of a scene. All cameras should stay on one side of this line so that screen direction remains consistent. 'Crossing the line' means placing the camera on the other side of the line — that is, breaking the rule. It should be avoided because it reverses the screen positions and direction of movement of the subjects, which confuses the audience about who is where and who is looking at whom.

subjective.question: Differentiate between pan and tilt camera movements.
subjective.answer: Pan is the horizontal movement of the camera — the camera turns left or right on its fixed mounting (tripod/pedestal) without changing its position. Tilt is the vertical movement of the camera — the camera tilts up or down on its fixed mounting. Both movements change only the direction in which the camera points, not the camera's position.

subjective.question: Differentiate between zooming and a dolly movement.
subjective.answer: Zooming changes the focal length of the zoom lens, so the subject appears to come closer or move away while the camera itself stays in one position; the perspective of the scene does not change. In a dolly movement the whole camera is physically moved towards or away from the subject on a dolly or track, so the camera position and the perspective of the scene actually change, giving a more natural effect.

subjective.question: What is a wide-angle lens? When is a wide-angle shot used?
subjective.answer: A wide-angle lens is a lens of short focal length that covers a wide area of the scene. A shot of a broad field of action taken with a wide-angle lens is called a wide-angle shot. It is used to show large settings, crowds and interiors, and to establish the overall scene, because it captures much more of the surroundings than a normal lens from the same position.

subjective.question: What is depth of field? Name the factors that affect it.
subjective.answer: Depth of field is the range of distances in front of the camera within which objects appear acceptably sharp in the image. It is affected by three main factors: (1) Aperture — a smaller aperture (higher f-number) increases depth of field, a wider aperture decreases it; (2) Focal length — a longer (telephoto) lens gives shallower depth of field than a wide-angle lens; (3) Camera-to-subject distance — the closer the camera is to the subject, the shallower the depth of field.

subjective.question: Differentiate between depth of field and depth perspective.
subjective.answer: Depth of field is the range of distances that appear acceptably sharp (in focus) in an image — it is a property of focus controlled by aperture, focal length and subject distance. Depth perspective, on the other hand, is the apparent distance of the foreground and background in relation to each other — the impression of depth or distance between objects in the frame as perceived by the viewer.

subjective.question: What is white balance? Why is it adjusted before recording?
subjective.answer: White balance is the adjustment of the camera so that white objects are recorded as truly white, without a colour cast, under different lighting conditions (such as daylight or tungsten light). It is adjusted before recording because different light sources have different colour temperatures; without correct white balance, all the colours in the picture would appear shifted — for example, whites would look blue or orange.

subjective.question: Explain three-point lighting, stating the function of each light.
subjective.answer: Three-point lighting is the standard lighting arrangement for a subject. It uses three lights: (1) Key light — the main, strongest light that illuminates the subject and defines its form and shadows; (2) Fill light — a softer light placed opposite the key light to soften and reduce the harsh shadows created by the key light; (3) Back light — placed behind the subject, it lights the subject's edges (hair and shoulders) and separates the subject from the background, giving depth to the picture.

subjective.question: What is broadcast style of writing? How does writing a video script differ from writing for print media?
subjective.answer: Broadcast style is a simple, clear and conversational style of writing meant to be heard rather than read: short sentences, simple words, present tense where possible, and one idea per sentence. Writers write video scripts in this style. A video script differs from print writing because it is written for the ear and the eye together — the words must match the visuals, timings are noted, and directions for camera, audio and graphics are included, usually in a two-column (video/audio) format.

subjective.question: What are demographics? How do they help in determining the acceptability of content for an audience?
subjective.answer: Demographics are the statistical characteristics of an audience, such as age, gender, income, education, occupation and family size. Broadcasters identify the demographics of their target audience to determine the acceptability of content — that is, to decide which programmes, language, themes and timings will be suitable and acceptable for that particular audience group.

subjective.question: What is PBS? How does public broadcasting differ from commercial broadcasting?
subjective.answer: PBS stands for Public Broadcasting Service, the public television network of the United States. Public broadcasting is non-commercial: it is funded mainly by government/public funds, grants and viewer support, and its aim is to inform, educate and serve the public interest. Commercial broadcasting, in contrast, is run for profit and earns its revenue mainly from advertisements (commercials) shown during and between programmes, so it focuses on attracting large audiences for advertisers.

subjective.question: Why do broadcasters try to hold the interest of the audience through the intervening commercials?
subjective.answer: Most broadcasting is commercial, and advertisers pay for the time (commercials) that interrupts the programmes. If viewers lose interest and switch channels during the intervening commercials, the advertisers' messages are not seen and the broadcaster loses revenue. Therefore the primary goal of most broadcasting is simply to hold the interest of the audience through the intervening commercials, so that viewers keep watching the programme — and the advertisements — until the end.

subjective.question: What is dialogue in a programme? How is the term used for music programmes?
subjective.answer: Dialogue is the spoken conversation between two or more characters or participants in a programme. In music programmes, a composition or passage written for two or more parts that is suggestive of conversational interplay — the parts answering and responding to each other like people talking — is called a dialogue. It creates the feeling of a musical conversation between the performers or instruments.

subjective.question: Why do music producers sometimes work long or irregular hours?
subjective.answer: Music production runs against fixed telecast and release schedules, and studio time, artists and sessions are booked for limited periods. When recordings, mixing or editing take longer than planned, music producers sometimes work long or irregular hours — late nights and extra sessions — to finish the work and meet the deadlines.

subjective.question: What is the theme of a programme? Why is it important?
subjective.answer: The theme of a programme is its central idea, subject or underlying message — what the programme is really about. All the elements of the programme — script, visuals, music and presentation — are organized around the theme so that the programme communicates one clear and unified idea to the audience.
